### Observed differences

- Work assignment was reallocated across at least six activities (A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, A22). In the earlier window, each of these activities was spread over a broad group of resources with the largest single shares around 7–13 in 100 (User_5 alone held about 10 in 100 of A01 and about 13 in 100 of A22); in the later window, a largely different group dominates — for example User_49 rose from no top-ten share to about 8 in 100 on A01 and about 10 in 100 on A22, while User_5 and the other earlier holders dropped out of the top shares [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006].
- The shift has the same shape in all six activities: one consistent group of about eight resources gains share in every one of them, a largely disjoint group of earlier holders loses share in every one of them, and the residual "other resources" share shrinks from roughly 42–47 in 100 to roughly 31–42 in 100. A13 and A14 show identical before/after profiles, so they likely reflect the same underlying reallocation rather than two independent changes [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006].
- A24 changed differently: in the earlier window its assignments were spread over 13 distinct resources, with the top resource, User_30, taking about 19 in 100; in the later window, User_30 handled every observed A24 assignment (top share 100 in 100, distinct resources down from 13 to 1, concentration index up from 0.11 to 1.0) [ASSIGN007, CONC001].
- The differences are large and unusual for random variation: the six activity profiles differ by 0.32–0.45 on the cosine-dissimilarity scale, A24 by 0.43 (assignments) and 0.89 (concentration index), and every item's difference exceeds about 1999 of 2000 random re-splits of the pooled data; the profiles rest on roughly 100–250 observations per window [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, CONC001].
- Screening context: all eight qualifying items are resource items, where only about 0.004 would be expected by chance; the control-flow family produced 0 items (about 0.18 expected) and the time family 0 items (about 0.02 expected), so no structural or timing difference reached the thresholds [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, CONC001].

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports a change in resource allocation as a specific possibility: across A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22, assignment work moved from a group of resources active in the earlier window to a largely different group in the later window, and A24 became handled exclusively by User_30, which previously carried only about 19 in 100 of its assignments [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, CONC001]. The signs are direct and consistent: the same gaining and losing groups repeat across all six activities, each difference is larger than about 1999 of 2000 random re-splits, the eight resource items compare with about 0.004 expected without change, and control flow and timing produced no qualifying items, so the difference is confined to allocation rather than to structure or timing [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, CONC001]. Limitations: the resource codes are anonymous, so the evidence shows reallocation between groups of resources but cannot show whether it reflects a changed assignment rule or simply a changed pool of available resources — the evidence cannot separate these two explanations; the six activity profiles may also partly express one shared reallocation rather than independent per-activity changes [ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004].

Other differences: none beyond the allocation items above; no control-flow or timing indicator qualified at the configured thresholds [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, CONC001].
